answer_text:
Interpret the sum in the usual discrete sense, taking \(x\) through integer values (in fact even integers suffice). Let

\[
n=x,\qquad j=2k.
\]

Then the expression becomes

\[
E_n=
\frac{\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le n\\ j\ \text{even}}}\binom{n}{j}j(n-j)}
{\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le n\\ j\ \text{even}}}\binom{n}{j}(n-j)^2}.
\]

We will evaluate the two sums over even \(j\).

---

### 1. Separate even-indexed terms

For any sequence \(a_j\),

\[
\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le n\\ j\ \text{even}}} a_j
=
\frac12\sum_{j=0}^n a_j+\frac12\sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j a_j.
\]

So it suffices to compute the ordinary sums and show the alternating sums vanish.

---

### 2. The alternating sums vanish for large \(n\)

Both summands are quadratic polynomials in \(j\):

\[
j(n-j)=nj-j^2,
\qquad
(n-j)^2=n^2-2nj+j^2.
\]

From

\[
(1+t)^n=\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}t^j,
\]

evaluating at \(t=-1\) and differentiating gives, for \(n\ge 3\),

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j\binom{n}{j}=0,
\]

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n j(-1)^j\binom{n}{j}=0,
\]

and from the second derivative,

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n j(j-1)(-1)^j\binom{n}{j}=0.
\]

Since \(j^2=j(j-1)+j\), any quadratic polynomial in \(j\) has vanishing alternating binomial sum for \(n\ge 3\). Therefore,

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j\binom{n}{j}j(n-j)=0,
\]

and

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j\binom{n}{j}(n-j)^2=0.
\]

Thus the even-indexed sums are exactly half of the full sums:

\[
\sum_{j\ \text{even}}\binom{n}{j}j(n-j)
=
\frac12\sum_{j=0}^n\binom{n}{j}j(n-j),
\]

\[
\sum_{j\ \text{even}}\binom{n}{j}(n-j)^2
=
\frac12\sum_{j=0}^n\binom{n}{j}(n-j)^2.
\]

---

### 3. Compute the full binomial sums

We use the standard identities

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n j\binom{n}{j}=n2^{n-1},
\]

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n j(j-1)\binom{n}{j}=n(n-1)2^{n-2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n j^2\binom{n}{j}
=
\sum_{j=0}^n j(j-1)\binom{n}{j}
+
\sum_{j=0}^n j\binom{n}{j}
\]

\[
=
n(n-1)2^{n-2}+n2^{n-1}
=
n(n+1)2^{n-2}.
\]

Now,

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}j(n-j)
=
n\sum_{j=0}^n j\binom{n}{j}
-
\sum_{j=0}^n j^2\binom{n}{j}.
\]

Substituting,

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}j(n-j)
=
n\cdot n2^{n-1}-n(n+1)2^{n-2}.
\]

Factor out \(2^{n-2}\):

\[
=2^{n-2}\bigl(2n^2-n(n+1)\bigr)
=
2^{n-2}n(n-1).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{j\ \text{even}}\binom{n}{j}j(n-j)
=
\frac12 n(n-1)2^{n-2}
=
n(n-1)2^{n-3}.
\]

For the denominator, by symmetry \(j\mapsto n-j\),

\[
\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}(n-j)^2
=
\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}j^2
=
n(n+1)2^{n-2}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\sum_{j\ \text{even}}\binom{n}{j}(n-j)^2
=
\frac12 n(n+1)2^{n-2}
=
n(n+1)2^{n-3}.
\]

---

### 4. Take the ratio

Hence for \(n\ge 3\),

\[
E_n
=
\frac{n(n-1)2^{n-3}}{n(n+1)2^{n-3}}
=
\frac{n-1}{n+1}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty} E_x
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n-1}{n+1}
=
1.
\]

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
